stories.title: Terreno Adds to NYC Portfolio with Red Hook Acquisition
stories.excerpt: Terreno Realty Corporation, a Bellevue, WA-based owner and operator of industrial real estate, acquired an industrial property located in Red Hook Brooklyn, for approximately $26.3 million. The seller was not identified. Located at 659 Court St., the property consists of one industrial distribution building containing approximately 28,000 square feet on 1.5 acres. It provides two grade-level loading positions and parking for 70 cars. The property has riparian access and is 100% leased to a maritime goods and services provider. The estimated stabilized cap rate is 5.2%. Terreno acquires, owns and operates industrial real estate in six major coastal U.S. markets: New York City/Northern New Jersey, Los Angeles, Miami, San Francisco Bay Area, Seattle and Washington, DC. Its NYC/NJ portfolio now encompasses 69 properties totaling nearly 3.6 million square feet, making it the largest by building count among the six markets. The post Terreno Adds to NYC Portfolio with Red Hook Acquisition appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Terreno Realty acquires Red Hook Brooklyn industrial property for $26.3M at 5.2% cap rate.
NYC/NJ portfolio now 69 properties, 3.6M SF—largest by count among Terreno's six coastal markets.
100% leased to maritime goods provider; riparian access and 28k SF on 1.5 acres.
stories.summary: Terreno Realty, a Bellevue-based industrial REIT, acquired a fully leased 28,000-square-foot industrial property in Red Hook, Brooklyn for $26.3 million at a 5.2% cap rate. The property offers riparian access and serves a maritime goods and services tenant. Terreno's NYC/NJ portfolio now comprises 69 properties totaling 3.6 million square feet, making it the operator's largest market by property count among its six coastal U.S. markets.
stories.impact: Limited direct impact to multifamily development. Industrial acquisitions at 5.2% cap rates signal compressed returns across coastal CRE, but this is a pure logistics/warehouse play. Relevant only if it indicates capital competition for Brooklyn real estate or signals strong waterfront demand that might influence mixed-use or residential waterfront valuations in Brooklyn.

stories.title: Building Block Foundation Fund: CRE Industry’s Way to Make a Difference
stories.excerpt: Presented by Bob O’Neill, executive vice president, CapRock Partners, Building Block Foundation Fund Boardmember. CapRock is also Endless Summer Title Sponsor. Why should people get involved with Building Block Foundation Fund? Building Block Foundation Fund is a nonprofit organized by volunteer professionals from across the commercial real estate industry. Our fundraising efforts involve bringing people together to network and spend time with their CRE peers – which makes Building Block unique. There are several Orange County charities with compelling missions, and they draw from supporters from across the entire Southern California and Orange County business and corporate spectrum, so those charity event attendees are not necessarily building business connections with people focused in their industry. We are 100% commercial real estate focused, which is a key reason why CRE industry people should support Building Block. What inspired your involvement with Building Block Foundation Fund? I had a friend who was on the board who invited me to get involved. While I was considering joining the board, three thoughts came to mind: I have an extensive business network, I’m not afraid to ask the question of people to support our mission, and I knew I could make a difference in the communities and charities that we donate to. It also matters to CapRock Partners because one of our seven core values is ‘Blessed to be a Blessing.” Our principals set aside 10% of partner profits to reinvest in the communities where we invest and develop. Building Block is an important part of that goal. How does Building Block choose its charities? There’s a great deal of need in Orange County. Everywhere you look, there are multiple charities doing great work, but unfortunately, we can’t support all of them. bullets: Building Block Foundation Fund is nonprofit charity fundraiser organized by CRE industry volunteers.
Focuses on Orange County area charities; CapRock Partners EVP Bob O'Neill involved.
Networking-driven model connects CRE professionals to support community missions.
stories.summary: Building Block Foundation Fund is a nonprofit organized by volunteer CRE industry professionals to raise capital for Orange County charities. CapRock Partners EVP Bob O'Neill serves on the board. The fund's model differentiates itself by creating industry-specific networking and fundraising opportunities for CRE peers supporting local charitable missions.
stories.impact: No material impact to multifamily development strategy, underwriting, or capital markets. This is industry philanthropic infrastructure unrelated to demand, supply, costs, or financing for apartment communities.

stories.title: Prism Partners Trades Two-Building Edison Lofts for $131M
stories.excerpt: Cushman & Wakefield arranged the $131-million investment sale of Edison Lofts, a 334-unit luxury multifamily community with nearly 19,000 square feet of retail space at 33 Ashland Ave. in West Orange, NJ. The Cushman & Wakefield team of Niko Nicolaou, Ryan Dowd, JP Hohl, Michael Guerra, Kelly Kellett and Alexandria Russo Ebers represented both the seller, Prism Partners and its capital partners, and the buyer, Sym Investments. Cushman & Wakefield’s Equity, Debt & Structured Finance team of John Alascio, Brad Domenico, and Chuck Kohaut arranged a $91.7-million acquisition loan featuring a full-term interest-only structure from New York Life. “Edison Lofts attracted significant investor interest because it offers a combination that is increasingly difficult to replicate in today’s market,” said Nicolaou. “The property delivers the character of a historic conversion with the scale, amenities and accessibility that continue to resonate with today’s renters. Coupled with strong occupancy and a favorable tax pilot, it represented a rare opportunity to acquire a well-positioned multifamily asset in one of Northern New Jersey’s most active investment markets.” Edison Lofts comprises two residential buildings totaling 334 apartments. The community includes The Residences at Edison Lofts, a 300-unit conversion of the historic Thomas Edison Battery Building, a former manufacturing building, and The Mews at Edison Lofts, a 34-unit ground-up residential building. The post Prism Partners Trades Two-Building Edison Lofts for $131M appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Prism Partners sells Edison Lofts (334 units, luxury, West Orange NJ) to Sym Investments for $131M.
New York Life provides $91.7M acquisition loan, full-term interest-only structure.
Property includes 19k SF retail; historic conversion with strong occupancy and tax PILOT incentive.
stories.summary: Prism Partners sold Edison Lofts, a 334-unit luxury multifamily community in West Orange, New Jersey, to Sym Investments for $131 million. The transaction was facilitated by Cushman & Wakefield, which also arranged a $91.7 million acquisition loan from New York Life featuring a full-term interest-only structure. The property comprises two historic residential buildings with 19,000 square feet of retail space and benefits from a favorable tax PILOT.
stories.impact: West Orange, NJ—strong pricing and debt availability for well-positioned historic conversions signals continued investor appetite for character-plus-scale assets near NYC. The interest-only structure and tax abatement support higher LTV execution; developers should prioritize adaptive reuse conversion platforms in Northern NJ submarkets within 15 miles of Manhattan to capture similar pricing and financing tailwinds before cap rates harden.

stories.title: $67M Refinancing Secured by JLL for Seniors Housing Property in Kansas
stories.excerpt: JLL arranged a $66.875 million refinancing for The Fieldston, a 209-unit luxury active adult multifamily community in Fairway, Kansas. JLL worked on behalf of the borrower, a partnership between EPC Real Estate Group and Platform Ventures, to secure the five-year construction take-out loan. The JLL Capital Markets Debt Advisory team representing the borrower was led by Managing Director Mark Erland, Senior Director Kevin Baron and Associate Ellie Savage. Completed in 2025, The Fieldston spans 4.64 acres at 4210 Shawnee Mission Parkway and is uniquely positioned as the only luxury active-adult community serving the North Johnson County submarket. Units are available in one-, two- and three-bedroom layouts. “With 28% of the population within a three-mile radius of Fieldston over 55 years old and no other Class A active adult properties within the same radius, this luxury property taps into an affluent, underserved market segment, promising strong demand and sustained occupancy,” said Erland. The post $67M Refinancing Secured by JLL for Seniors Housing Property in Kansas appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: JLL secures $66.875M five-year construction take-out loan for The Fieldston, Fairway, Kansas.
209-unit luxury active-adult community completed 2025; EPC Real Estate Group and Platform Ventures partnership.
North Johnson County: 28% population 55+ within 3-mile radius; only Class A active-adult property in submarket.
stories.summary: JLL arranged a $66.875 million five-year construction take-out loan for The Fieldston, a 209-unit luxury active-adult multifamily community completed in 2025 in Fairway, Kansas. Developed by partnership between EPC Real Estate Group and Platform Ventures, the property spans 4.64 acres and offers one-, two-, and three-bedroom units. The submarket is uniquely positioned with 28% of the population over 55 years old within a three-mile radius and no competing Class A active-adult properties.
stories.impact: North Johnson County, Kansas—senior housing development momentum with institutional-grade debt execution signals lender confidence in age-restricted demand fundamentals in secondary metros. Developers should identify similar demographic-supply imbalances (affluent, aging, no Class A senior option) in Midwest and Sun Belt secondary markets; this playbook is scalable and appears to command favorable debt terms from conservative lenders seeking seasoned sponsors.

stories.title: Rhode Island Healthcare Portfolio Secures $30M FHA/HUD Refi
stories.excerpt: Greystone has provided $30,260,600 in FHA/HUD-insured financing for the refinance of a four-property healthcare portfolio in Rhode Island. The financing was originated by Christopher Clare and Ryan Harkins, with additional team members including David Young, Ben Rubin, Parker Nielsen and Liam Gallagher. The portfolio includes four skilled nursing facilities totaling 385 beds across Rhode Island. Greystone previously provided bridge financing for the portfolio, positioning the borrower to transition to long-term FHA/HUD-insured financing. The refi supports the borrower’s long-term ownership strategy by replacing interim bridge debt with stable, lower-cost financing through HUD. “Greystone’s integrated platform continues to deliver financing solutions that support both immediate refinancing needs and long-term strategic goals,” said Harkins. “This transaction reflects our commitment to helping healthcare operators optimize performance while securing durable, lower-cost capital through HUD execution.” The post Rhode Island Healthcare Portfolio Secures $30M FHA/HUD Refi appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Greystone provides $30.26M FHA/HUD-insured refi for four-property Rhode Island skilled nursing portfolio.
385 beds total across four SNF properties; bridge debt replaced with stable, long-term HUD financing.
Borrower transitions from interim financing to durable, lower-cost capital structure through HUD program.
stories.summary: Greystone originated $30.26 million in FHA/HUD-insured refinancing for a four-property healthcare portfolio comprising skilled nursing facilities totaling 385 beds across Rhode Island. The financing replaced interim bridge debt and was positioned as part of the borrower's long-term ownership strategy. The transaction reflects a shift from short-term interim capital to stable, lower-cost government-backed debt.
stories.impact: Limited direct multifamily relevance; however, HUD refinancing on healthcare real estate signals strong government appetite for seasoned operators with proven occupancy. Developers with diverse multifamily and healthcare portfolios should note that HUD execution timelines remain competitive and that nursing/senior housing platforms continue to attract institutional capital—cross-asset opportunities remain underexplored for multifamily operators.

stories.title: OCVibe’s Scott Frick On Building a $5B District Around Anaheim’s Honda Center
stories.excerpt: A 100-acre master-planned development is turning the sea of parking lots surrounding Anaheim’s Honda Center into a dense mixed-use district where people can live, work and eat whether or not the Ducks are playing. Henry and Susan Samueli, owners of the National Hockey League’s Anaheim Ducks, are privately financing the large development named OCVibe. Scott Frick, senior vice president of real estate and district operations at the Samueli’s Orange County Sports & Entertainment, is managing the project, and described it as a $5 billion investment with 170,000 square feet of office space, more than 2,000 apartments, two hotels and more than 35 dining concepts. The broader plan also includes 20 acres of parks and plazas. The first major public-facing pieces are scheduled to arrive in 2027, including Katella Commons, a 50,000-square-foot market hall, along with a 5,000-capacity concert venue, and The Weave, a six-story mass-timber office building where flexible-office operator Kiln has committed to a full floor. Then the Honda Center will host indoor volleyball during the 2028 Olympics, when Frick expects roughly half a million people to pass through the arena in 11 days. Commercial Observer spoke with Frick about how the absence of outside investors changes the economics, OCVibe’s office and residential strategy, and how to keep restaurants busy when the arena goes dark. The conversation has been edited for length and clarity.   Commercial Observer: Can you give an overview of where construction stands today? Scott Frick: We started construction about three years ago. We’ll be delivering phases through about 2030, 2031. The first phase was really building parking structures to free up the surface lots. Honda Center is a very typical suburban arena. It’s kind of in the middle of nowhere, surrounded by surface parking and industrial uses. bullets: OCVibe: $5B master-planned district around Anaheim Honda Center; 2,000+ apartments, 170k SF office, 2 hotels.
100 acres, privately financed by Henry and Susan Samueli (Ducks owners); major deliveries begin 2027.
Katella Commons (50k SF market hall), 5k-cap concert venue, six-story mass-timber office (Kiln operator) launching 2027.
stories.summary: OCVibe, a $5 billion master-planned development surrounding Anaheim's Honda Center, will transform 100 acres of parking lots into a dense mixed-use district. Privately financed by Ducks owners Henry and Susan Samueli, the project includes more than 2,000 apartments, 170,000 square feet of office, two hotels, 20 acres of parks and plazas, and 35+ dining concepts. First major components arrive in 2027, including a 50,000-square-foot market hall, 5,000-capacity concert venue, and mass-timber office building.
stories.impact: Anaheim/Orange County—massive, privately-capitalized residential pipeline (2,000+ units) entering market 2027 onward will intensify competitive pressure on existing multifamily in Orange County coastal submarkets and reshape Anaheim's demand profile from event-driven to year-round urban living. Developers should monitor delivery pacing and pre-leasing strategy; if Samueli front-loads amenity/office delivery before residential, downtown revitalization may pull renters away from traditional Orange County infill. Consider counter-positioning in premium coastal markets (Huntington, Newport) or identifying acquisition targets in path-of-growth corridors south/east of Anaheim before land prices inflate.

stories.title: Pinnacle Group Sells Rights to Upper West Side Apartment Tower for $88M
stories.excerpt: Pinnacle Group has offloaded another asset, this time on Manhattan’s Upper West Side. The prominent New York City landlord, which put a massive rent-stabilized portfolio into bankruptcy last year, sold its rights to an apartment building at 323 West 96th Street to private real estate company Lightstone Group for approximately $88 million, according to a source with knowledge of the deal. The Real Deal first reported the sale, citing filings by Pinnacle’s parent company, Zarasai Group, with the Tel Aviv Stock Exchange. The filings, dated Aug. 13, announced the successfully completed sale of Pinnacle’s 100 percent interest in the 15-story building’s lease rights and a 50 percent hold on the land rights. Daniel Parker, Gary Phillips and Will Silverman at Eastdil Secured Savills advised on the deal. An $11 million surplus from the sale is slated to be deposited into the account of Series C bondholders. A spokesperson for Pinnacle Group could not be reached for comment on the most recent sale. The property carried an existing loan balance of about $65 million as of late March, last transferred from Starwood Mortgage Capital to a Barclays-sponsored commercial mortgage-backed securities (CMBS) trust in 2023. Pinnacle secured the leasehold to 323 West 96th Street in 2007, according to city records, and paid another $27 million for its land rights stake in 2016. The 173-unit apartment building, built in 2001, sits at the corner of East 96th Street and First Avenue. The sale comes days after news that Pinnacle offloaded a $128 million condominium and commercial portfolio spanning 39 transactions across Queens, Brooklyn and Manhattan. The buyer was Friar Park JW, an entity with links to Tremada Holdings, an affiliate of London-based property company William Pears Group. Pinnacle, led by Joel Wiener, placed a portfolio of roughly 5,000 rent-stabilized apartments across New York City into bankruptcy in May 2025 after facing approximately $574.4 million in debt. bullets: Pinnacle Group sells 323 West 96th Street (Manhattan UWS) lease rights to Lightstone Group for $88M.
15-story apartment building; Pinnacle retains 50% land rights; $11M surplus to Series C bondholders.

stories.summary: Pinnacle Group sold its 100% interest in the lease rights to a 15-story apartment building at 323 West 96th Street on Manhattan's Upper West Side to Lightstone Group for approximately $88 million. Pinnacle retained a 50% interest in the land rights. The sale generated an $11 million surplus slated for Series C bondholders and follows Pinnacle's bankruptcy filing on its larger rent-stabilized portfolio last year.
stories.impact: Manhattan Upper West Side—distressed seller (Pinnacle post-bankruptcy) unloading prime Manhattan residential at $88M for 100% lease rights signals capital relief over value optimization, but sale price and Lightstone's acquisition indicate Manhattan residential fundamentals remain strong enough to attract opportunistic buyers willing to take on stabilized rent-regulated exposure. Developers should monitor whether Lightstone repositions building post-stabilization or holds for long-term cash flow; either way, UWS multifamily demand remains resilient and justifies acquisition by quality operators even at premium basis.

stories.title: At New York City Council Hearing on Pied-à-Terre Tax, Complaints of a Sloppy Rollout
stories.excerpt: As a legal battle over New York’s pied-à-terre tax continues, the New York City Council held a hearing Tuesday evaluating the surcharge on second homes. Manhattan Councilmember Gale Brewer led the inquiry against what she saw as a dysfunctional rollout of the tax that included publishing up to 900,000 names and addresses of possible second homes in the five boroughs. The Mamdani administration did not send any representatives to the hearing at City Hall, including from the Department of Finance tasked with collecting the tax. The hearing was held by the Committee on Finance and the Committee on Governmental Operations, State and Federal Legislation. “No estimate of the number of pied-à-terres in the city comes even close to 900,000,” Brewer said. “Yet, the city still published the list with the small caveat that the properties on the list may be subject to the charge. The list published by the Department of Finance was so overbroad that it even included my name, and I don’t mind my name and my home address [being included], but I’ve been in that home 365 days a year since 1994. I don’t leave the city, and I don’t have a second home.” The committee hoped to get answers from the Mamdani administration on why — when it had credible information from the New York City Comptroller‘s office about how many second homes there are — it still attempted to force thousands of property owners in the city to prove that the addresses are primary residences. Brewer stated that the “onus” should not have been on the homeowners, but on the city to determine whether the home is a primary residence. “Homeowners who believe that they received the letters in error initially had only a short window to contest the surcharge,” Brewer said. “ Although the deadline was ultimately extended by four weeks, this still puts the burden on property owners, which upset people tremendously.” About 17,000 homeowners received letters informing them that they are on the suppl
bullets: NYC Council hearing on pied-à-terre tax; criticism of sloppy rollout and overbroad 900k-property list.
Councilmember Brewer cites dysfunctional implementation; Mamdani administration did not attend hearing.
Legal battle ongoing; tax compliance and administration remain in flux.
stories.summary: New York City Council held a hearing Tuesday on the pied-à-terre tax, a surcharge on second homes. Manhattan Councilmember Gale Brewer led criticism of the tax's rollout, specifically the Department of Finance's publication of up to 900,000 property names and addresses—significantly overbroad, according to officials. The Mamdani administration did not send representatives to the hearing, and legal challenges to the tax remain active.
stories.impact: Manhattan/NYC—pied-à-terre tax remains legally and administratively uncertain; regulatory dysfunction creates near-term soft-demand headwind for luxury/investment condo development but long-term housing supply implications minimal since tax targets only second homes, not primary multifamily rentals. Developers should monitor court rulings and administration refinement of implementation; a clarified, narrowly-applied tax would remove uncertainty and could modestly reduce investor-buyer competition for trophy assets in Manhattan, creating windows for owner-occupant multifamily conversion opportunities.

stories.title: Betting on South Beach Luxury Shopping, Vivienne Westwood Plans to Open Store
stories.excerpt: Vivienne Westwood is finally getting serious about opening a boutique in Miami’s South Beach. Almost two years after buying the three-story property at 736 Collins Avenue and letting it sit vacant, the luxury fashion brand has submitted an application to build out the property, which dates back to 1921. The 4,356-square-foot ground-floor space would feature a store with three fittings rooms and two storage rooms. The second floor would house executive offices and meeting rooms, while the top floor would include a bridal showroom and rooftop deck. A neon sign would be mounted onto the entrance wall. The project “honors the building’s 1921 Art Deco and Mediterranean Revival heritage while introducing contemporary elements,” wrote Daniel Gabay, who runs National Permit Group and filed the proposal. The modern elements include “Florida limestone cladding, polished brass storefront and motifs, a rigid canopy reinterpreting the documented historic faux eave, a landmark pink neon signature, and the iconic Orb statue in the forecourt,” per the application, which Miami Beach Historic Preservation Board will consider next month. In 2024, the British brand paid $6 million for the 14,692-square-foot building located just a few blocks west of Ocean Drive, sandwiched between Seventh and Eighth Streets. Unlike most luxury labels of its size, it remains independent under the ownership of Vivienne Westwood’s family. The namesake designer passed away in 2022. Vivienne Westwood, the brand, is betting that high-end retail will return to the heart of South Beach. In the 1990s and 2000s, the area housed boutiques from the likes of Versace, Hugo Boss and Barney’s. But almost all shuttered, opting instead to open outposts at the Bal Harbour Shops up north and the Design District out west, which have become some of the highest-grossing upscale malls in the country. Julia Echikson can be reached at jechikson@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Vivienne Westwood submits permit to build out 736 Collins Avenue, Miami South Beach (4,356 SF ground floor).
Three-story 1921 Art Deco building; purchased ~2 years ago, vacant until now; bridal showroom, offices, rooftop.
Retail-focused buildout; honors historic facade while adding contemporary Florida limestone and neon signage.
stories.summary: Vivienne Westwood submitted a permit application to build out its three-story property at 736 Collins Avenue in Miami's South Beach, a 1921 Art Deco building purchased approximately two years ago and left vacant. The 4,356-square-foot ground floor will house a retail boutique with fitting and storage rooms; the second floor will contain executive offices; the third floor will feature a bridal showroom and rooftop deck. The design honors the building's historic Art Deco character while introducing contemporary elements.
stories.impact: Miami South Beach—luxury retail activation on Collins Avenue signals sustained high-end consumer spending and commercial confidence in South Beach's long-term appeal, but this is a retail/hospitality story with minimal direct multifamily demand signal. Relevant only as demand-side proxy: if Westwood is betting on South Beach foot traffic and demographics, mixed-use residential development nearby (commercial ground floor + upper residential) may justify higher-density approvals. Monitor whether South Beach commercial recovery attracts multifamily conversion or new-build projects.

stories.title: Get to Know the Broker: Vickey Barron of Compass
stories.excerpt: Vickey Barron, an associate broker at Compass, knows how to get deals done — and all with the perfect mix of intelligence, charm, charisma and a take-no-nonsense attitude. It’s what makes her one of the best real estate brokers in the business. Barron, 69, has worked on more than 600 sales during her career and earned a slew of awards, including the Real Estate Board of New York’s Rookie of the Year award in 2001 and the board’s Eileen Spinola Distinguished Service Award in 2015. Barron has done an endless amount of million-dollar deals, but for her, the value of her job isn’t money — it’s the difference she can make in someone’s life. “People always want me to talk about commissions and big sales, and I just am a strong believer that our purpose in this role of real estate is not money and commission and who has the biggest numbers,” Barron said. “It’s really about serving people.” Commercial Observer caught up with Barron in August for a new series called “Get to Know the Broker,” where we connect with residential brokers to learn more about what makes them tick. This conversation has been edited for length and clarity. Commercial Observer: What was the biggest deal of your career? Vickey Barron: Ironically, this is not the one with the highest sale price or largest commission. In our business, there tends to be an emphasis on the commissions and money earned, but, going back to basics, we are in the business of helping people find homes and find solace. My biggest and most important deal was helping a 93-year-old woman negotiate a life estate so she could remain in her West Village townhouse after the sale took place. Sometimes we get caught up and forget that we’re all human and we age. Life has chapters, and our contributions matter. This deal had the biggest and most positive impact in my career. What is your career Everest? When clients know they can count on me, they stay loyal for years. Trust is what keeps the phone ringing — that’s the s
bullets: Profile: Vickey Barron, Compass associate broker; 69 years old, 600+ career sales since 2001.
Won REBNY Rookie of the Year 2001, Eileen Spinola Distinguished Service Award 2015.
Emphasizes client service over commission; primarily NYC residential brokerage focus.
stories.summary: Vickey Barron is an associate broker at Compass with a 23-year career and more than 600 completed sales. She received REBNY Rookie of the Year in 2001 and the Eileen Spinola Distinguished Service Award in 2015. Barron prioritizes client service over commission-driven sales and has built a reputation in New York residential brokerage.
stories.impact: No material impact to multifamily development. This is a career profile of a NYC residential sales broker; no market data, transaction intelligence, or policy signals relevant to development strategy, capital, supply, or demand.
